title: Dorothy and Termite: Oscar Breakouts Chart New Course for Indian Cinema at TIFF
excerpt: Oscar-winner Guneet Monga Kapoor premiered the Tamil gangster western “Dorothy” to a standing ovation at TIFF 2026 — her first project under Jio Studios' majority stake — while documentarian Shaunak Sen unveiled his fiction debut “Termite.”
body:
• Oscar-winner Guneet Monga Kapoor premiered “Dorothy,” a Tamil-language gangster western directed by Karthik Subbaraj, at TIFF 2026 — her first project since Jio Studios took a majority stake in Sikhya Entertainment.
  • “Dorothy” earned a standing ovation at its world premiere at Toronto’s Scotiabank Theatre and is the first Indian Tamil film to premiere at TIFF in a decade. It releases in cinemas worldwide on September 25, 2026.
  • Oscar-nominated documentarian Shaunak Sen unveiled “Termite,” his fiction directorial debut — a poetic short about a Delhi exterminator, shot in five days.
  • Their parallel career pivots signal a shift in Indian independent cinema: studio-backed regional films aimed at global festivals, and documentary auteurs moving into fiction.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=TE4osi30qGI

Two of Indian cinema’s Oscar-recognized talents arrived at the Toronto International Film Festival this week with career pivots that say as much about where the industry is headed as about the films themselves.

Producer Guneet Monga Kapoor, an Academy Award winner, premiered “Dorothy” — a Tamil-language gangster western set in 1990s rural Tamil Nadu, directed by Karthik Subbaraj — while documentarian Shaunak Sen, nominated for an Oscar for “All That Breathes,” unveiled “Termite,” his first fiction film.

“Dorothy”: Tamil cinema’s decade-defining festival moment

“Dorothy” had its world premiere in TIFF’s Centrepiece section at the Scotiabank Theatre, where it received a standing ovation. It is the first Indian Tamil film to premiere at TIFF in a decade — and the first major-festival premiere for Subbaraj, whose previous nine features, including “Jigarthanda” and “Mercury,” went straight to theatrical release.

The film stars Keerthy Suresh alongside relative newcomers Rishikanth and Sananth — a deliberate departure from the South Indian superstars Subbaraj typically casts — and features a score by the legendary Ilaiyaraaja, marking the composer’s 1,540th film. Two songs from the film, “Kalyana Virundhu” and “Muthumani,” have each crossed 10 million views on YouTube and featured among YouTube India’s top-five trending music videos.

“Dorothy is a story that comes from a place and culture I know intimately, but its questions around friendship, prejudice and human connection are universal.”

— Karthik Subbaraj, writer-director

The project is also the first from Sikhya Entertainment since Jio Studios acquired a majority stake in the company earlier this year. Jio Studios president Jyoti Deshpande framed the premiere as a milestone: “Dorothy is a powerful example” of cinema crossing languages when “the emotion at its centre is universal,” she said, calling it “a proud moment for Tamil cinema.” The 41-day principal shoot wrapped in rural Madurai in November and December 2025. The film opens in cinemas worldwide on September 25, 2026.

“Termite”: a documentarian turns to fiction

Sen’s “Termite” is a poetic short about a Delhi exterminator, shot in just five days — a radical change of scale for a filmmaker known for observational epics. The shift follows a period of upheaval: Sen was diagnosed with kidney cancer shortly after the 2023 Oscars, an experience that reshaped his slate.

He is now editing “The Delicate,” a documentary about vascular surgery begun after the diagnosis. And through KiteRabbit, the production company he runs with Aman Mann, Sen is co-producing a documentary with Joaquin Phoenix, Rooney Mara, and Jim Wilson, directed by Archana Phadke — a project Phoenix initiated after becoming a fan of “All That Breathes.”

A new financing map for Indian independents

Monga Kapoor and Subbaraj first met in 2016 on the awards circuit for “Visaaranai” and reconnected nearly a decade later, as she was building Sikhya’s slate with Jio and heard his pitch for “Dorothy.” That the first Sikhya project under Jio’s majority ownership is a Tamil gangster western — not the Hindi commercial fare Monga Kapoor’s Mumbai base might have suggested — signals the studio is using its backing for regionally rooted, festival-bound cinema.

Why the diaspora should pay attention

TIFF sits in a city with one of the world’s largest South Asian diasporas, and its Centrepiece programmers betting on a Tamil-language film — with a September 25 worldwide theatrical release — tests whether festival prestige can translate into box office beyond India. “Dorothy” and “Termite” also chart how Indian independent production now travels multiple financing paths at once: studio equity, international co-production, and festival launches feeding theatrical runs.

What comes next

“Dorothy” opens globally in less than two weeks. Its reception — both at TIFF and at the box office — will be watched as a test case for whether India’s studio-backed independent cinema can carry regional-language stories to worldwide audiences. For Sen, “Termite” marks a beginning: a documentarian entering fiction just as his subjects are entering some of the industry’s biggest rooms.
